title: Keystone Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Keystone wells have a median depth of 80 feet, with typical finished-well costs of $11,200-$20,000.
h1: Keystone, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For land and homes around Keystone, the available well records point to relatively shallow wells by mountain standards, but the geology still matters. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 80 feet, and the median reported yield is 12.0 gallons per minute.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That makes nearby well records useful for setting expectations, but not a guarantee for a particular lot. Before buying or building, review the permit, construction, water-rights requirements, septic layout, and neighboring wells with a Colorado contractor or water professional.

sections.heading: Keystone well depth reflects shallow mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Keystone is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 49 to 150 feet, so a driller bidding a typical lot may be working in that range rather than automatically planning a very deep hole. The 90th-percentile depth is 218 feet, and the deepest record reaches 550 feet.

Depth records are concentrated at the shallow end: 57% are under 100 feet, while 39% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 4% are between 300 and 600 feet, with 0% at 600 feet or more. Those figures help compare bids, but fractured granite and gneiss can change the result quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: What Keystone wells produce
sections.html:
Reported well yields are generally useful for household planning. The median is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Among wells with yield records, 53% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 43% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 0% report under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for a buyer, but a good well test still matters. Pumping capacity, storage, pressure equipment, and the permitted use all affect how comfortably a home can operate. Do not treat a nearby yield as a promise for an unbuilt well.

sections.heading: Keystone water levels and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 29 wells in the records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Within that group, the median depth to water is 30 feet, with the middle half from 25 to 60 feet. This gives a useful starting point for pump and trench discussions, not a site-specific water-table measurement.

The permit counts by decade do not establish a water-level trend. They show permitting activity, not water-level measurements: 27 permits in the 1960s, 44 in the 1970s, 77 in the 1980s, 149 in the 1990s, 116 in the 2000s, 42 in the 2010s, and 31 in the 2020s. A current well test and site evaluation are more useful than assuming the water table is rising or dropping.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Keystone, and when
sections.html:
Permit records extend through the newest permit year of 2025. The busiest names in this local record set are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 75 wells; Buena Vista Drilling, associated with Shelton, William L, with 68; and Arrow Drilling Co., associated with Berglund, Paul R., with 42.

The permit history is concentrated in the 1980s through the 2000s, with 77 permits in the 1980s, 149 in the 1990s, and 116 in the 2000s. Treat these names as a starting point for checking local experience and references, not as a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and who will handle the pump and electrical work.

sections.heading: Keystone well drilling cost at the recorded median depth
sections.html:
Keystone drilling runs through fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 80 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $5,200 to $8,000.

A finished well is more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled total is about $11,200 to $20,000 at that depth. A bid can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grouting requirements change, or the site needs unusual trenching. Ask for drilling, casing, development, pump, power, and testing as separate line items.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building in Keystone
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply over short distances. A lot may produce less than a nearby well, require more drilling, or encounter a dry hole. Review the nearest permits and construction reports, then ask for a written contingency plan. The local records show 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 907 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles.

Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular property. Test existing water for the contaminants relevant to the site and inspect well casing, grout, storage, and the pressure system. A septic designer must also confirm separation distances, soil conditions, and a workable drainfield location before a building envelope is finalized.

sections.heading: A practical Keystone lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby parcels. Confirm the permitted use: 65% of the local permits are domestic or household, 1% are stock, 0% are irrigation, and 10% are monitoring. A domestic permit does not automatically solve every water-rights or land-use question, especially in a mountain basin.

For a new build near Montezuma, Dillon, Breckenridge, Frisco, Silverthorne, or Blue River, price access and utilities along with drilling. Have a driller review the road, pad, casing, pump setting, and power route before closing. If the lot depends on a new well, make the purchase contingent on permit review, septic feasibility, and a defined drilling and water-quality testing plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Keystone, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Keystone is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 49 to 150 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 218 feet. Most records are under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 550 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can make one lot differ substantially from another.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Keystone?
faq.a: At the local median depth of 80 feet, the modeled drilled-hole cost is about $5,200 to $8,000 at $65 to $100 per foot. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $11,200 to $20,000. Difficult access, deeper drilling, casing, grouting, or unusual utility work can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Keystone wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield near Keystone is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Among wells reporting yield, 53% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 43% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. These records guide expectations but do not guarantee a new well's result.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Keystone, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and test results. The area has 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 907 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination on a specific property. Test the well, inspect construction, and review nearby environmental information before relying on the water.

faq.q: Can I build a house on a well near Keystone?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a promising nearby yield. Check the DWR permit, permitted use, well construction, water quality, septic feasibility, access, and utility route. Local records show 65% domestic or household permits and a median yield of 12.0 gallons per minute, but a new well can perform differently. Confirm requirements before closing or starting site work.
